title: Geometrical Optics: Lenses
short_intro: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by at least one curved spherical surface that refracts light to form real or virtual images. Lenses operate on the principle of Snell's Law of refraction at curved boundaries.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Refraction at spherical surfaces, lens maker's formula, thin lens formula, linear magnification, power of a lens, combination of thin lenses in contact, and simple optical instruments like magnifying glasses.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Lens displacement method (displacement method for focal length measurement), equivalent focal length of two lenses separated by a distance, thick lenses, chromatic and spherical aberrations in lenses, and cardinal points of optical systems.

prerequisites: Laws of reflection and refraction (Snell's Law)
Real and virtual images sign conventions (Cartesian sign convention)
Geometrical properties of triangles and spherical geometry

concept_notes.heading: Refraction at a Single Spherical Surface
bullets: Relates object distance (u), image distance (v), radius of curvature (R), refractive index of the medium containing the object (n<sub>1</sub>), and refractive index of the medium containing the image (n<sub>2</sub>).
Assumes paraxial ray approximation where angles of incidence and refraction are small.
Sign convention dictates distances measured against the direction of incident light are negative.

concept_notes.heading: Lens Maker's Formula and Thin Lenses
bullets: Relates the focal length (f) of a thin lens to the refractive index of the lens material (n) relative to the surrounding medium (n<sub>m</sub>) and the radii of curvature (R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>).
A double convex lens with n > n<sub>m</sub> converges light, whereas it diverges light if immersed in a medium with a higher refractive index than the lens.
The thin lens approximation assumes the thickness of the lens is negligible compared to object and image distances.

concept_notes.heading: Combination of Thin Lenses
bullets: For two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> in contact, the equivalent focal length F is given by 1/F = 1/f<sub>1</sub> + 1/f<sub>2</sub>.
The net power of lenses in contact is the algebraic sum of individual powers: P = P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub>.
When lenses are separated by a distance d, the equivalent focal length is modified to account for the spatial separation.

concept_notes.heading: Optical Aberrations in Lenses
bullets: Chromatic aberration arises due to the dependence of refractive index on wavelength (dispersion), causing different colors to focus at different points.
Spherical aberration occurs because marginal rays focus closer to the lens than paraxial rays for large apertures.
Can be minimized by using stopped-down apertures, crossed lenses, or a combination of suitable lenses.

derivations.title: Lens Maker's Formula
derivations.conditions: Thin lens of refractive index n<sub>2</sub> placed in a medium of refractive index n<sub>1</sub> with spherical surfaces of radii R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub>.
steps: Apply refraction formula for the first spherical surface: (n<sub>2</sub>/v<sub>1</sub>) - (n<sub>1</sub>/u) = (n<sub>2</sub> - n<sub>1</sub>)/R<sub>1</sub>, where v<sub>1</sub> is the intermediate image distance.
Treat the intermediate image as a virtual object for the second refracting surface: (n<sub>1</sub>/v) - (n<sub>2</sub>/v<sub>1</sub>) = (n<sub>1</sub> - n<sub>2</sub>)/R<sub>2</sub>.
Add the two equations to eliminate v<sub>1</sub>: (n<sub>1</sub>/v) - (n<sub>1</sub>/u) = (n<sub>2</sub> - n<sub>1</sub>)(1/R<sub>1</sub> - 1/R<sub>2</sub>).
Divide by n<sub>1</sub> and set u = -infinity and v = f to obtain the final expression.

derivations.title: Equivalent Focal Length of Two Thin Lenses Separated by Distance d
derivations.conditions: Two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> separated by distance d in air.
steps: Trace a paraxial ray parallel to the principal axis through the first lens to get deviation.
Determine the point of emergence from the second lens.
Apply the lens formula successively for each lens accounting for the coordinate shift d.
Equate the overall system to a single equivalent lens of focal length F.

graphs_and_experiments.title: u-v Graph for a Convex Lens
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular hyperbola plotted in the second quadrant for negative u and positive v, asymptotic to lines u = f and v = f.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the inverse nonlinear relation between object and image distances for a converging lens.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to find focal length graphically by finding the intercept where u = v = 2f.

graphs_and_experiments.title: 1/u vs 1/v Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line with a negative slope crossing the axes at 1/f.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Linearizes the thin lens equation (1/v - 1/u = 1/f) to yield intercept equal to 1/f.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Extensively used in laboratory optical bench experiments to determine focal length accurately.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Optical Bench Experiment for Convex Lens Focal Length
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup showing illuminated pin, lens holder, and movable screen on an optical bench scale.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Direct measurement of conjugate foci and displacement method parameters.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core practical component evaluated in viva voce and numerical problem formulation.

solved_numericals.question: A convex lens of glass (n = 1.5) has both surfaces of same radius of curvature R = 20 cm. Find its focal length in air.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: n = 1.5, R<sub>1</sub> = +20 cm, R<sub>2</sub> = -20 cm.
Substitute values into the lens maker's formula: 1/f = (1.5 - 1) * (1/20 - (-1/20)).

solved_numericals.question: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm and a concave lens of focal length 20 cm are placed in contact. Find the power and nature of the combination.
solution_steps: Identify focal lengths with signs: f<sub>1</sub> = +10 cm = +0.1 m, f<sub>2</sub> = -20 cm = -0.2 m.
Calculate individual powers: P<sub>1</sub> = 1 / (+0.1) = +10 D, P<sub>2</sub> = 1 / (-0.2) = -5 D.
Find net power: P = P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub> = +10 D - 5 D = +5 D.
Determine net focal length: F = 1 / P = +1/5 m = +20 cm.

solved_numericals.question: In a displacement method experiment, the distance between an object and a screen is 100 cm. A lens produces real images on the screen at two positions separated by 20 cm. Calculate the focal length of the lens.
solution_steps: Use the displacement method formula: f = (a<sup>2</sup> - d<sup>2</sup>) / (4a).
Substitute given values: a = 100 cm, d = 20 cm.

assumptions_and_limitations: Paraxial approximation (sin theta approx theta) holds true, limiting validity to small aperture lenses.
Thin lens approximation assumes thickness t approaches zero, ignoring refraction losses within the bulk material.
Monochromatic light is assumed unless chromatic dispersion is explicitly accounted for.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A convex lens always forms a real image.
common_misconceptions.correct: A convex lens forms a virtual image when the object is placed between the optical centre and the principal focus.
common_misconceptions.why: Ray divergence exceeds convergence capacity when the object is within the focal length.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The focal length of a glass lens remains unchanged if it is submerged in water.
common_misconceptions.correct: The focal length increases (power decreases) when a lens is immersed in water because the relative refractive index decreases.
common_misconceptions.why: Lens maker's formula depends on the ratio of refractive index of the lens to that of the surrounding medium.

quick_revision: A convex lens converges light in air and diverges it if placed in a medium of higher refractive index than itself.
